name: Green tea (Camellia sinensis) leaf extract
lead: Green tea leaf extract is a concentrate of polyphenols, mainly catechins such as epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), from unoxidized Camellia sinensis leaves. People use it in two ways for their looks: in creams and serums, where it is included as an antioxidant to help protect skin from the oxidative stress of UV exposure that drives visible ageing, and as an oral supplement, often alongside other ingredients in leanness and general-health stacks.[1][4]

A 2022 review of its phytochemistry and pharmacology lists antioxidant, antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activities, and notes it may assist treatment of dermatitis.[2] A 2015 review of herbal creams loaded with phyto-extracts, Camellia sinensis among them, summarises in vivo antioxidant studies and describes such formulations as possible cosmeceuticals for protecting skin against UV damage.[3]

Regulators and reviewers take a cautious view of oral extracts: Wikipedia reports that a 2011 European Food Safety Authority review found most proposed claims, including some on UV skin protection, not sufficiently supported, and that extracts have been associated with liver toxicity, leading Health Canada to recommend warning labels in 2017.[1]

chain: Catechins such as EGCG act as antioxidants

angle.text: Green tea extract is added to skincare as an antioxidant, with the aim of supporting skin that is less prone to visible sun-related ageing and irritation. Oral forms are taken by some as part of lean-physique supplement stacks.

infobox: Topical ointment approved in US (2006) for genital warts[1]

paras: Green tea is unfermented tea that keeps much of the natural content of fresh leaves. Its main polyphenols are four catechins: epicatechin, epicatechin gallate, epigallocatechin and EGCG, the most abundant and active.[5] Other constituents include alkaloids, amino acids and polysaccharides.[2] Brewed tea is mostly water, while supplement extracts can contain up to about 17% caffeine by weight.[1]
Matcha, a shade-grown powdered green tea, is described in a review as the most concentrated source of catechins, along with theanine and chlorophyll.[5]

In cosmetics, green tea extract is promoted as an antioxidant and soothing ingredient. Reviews of plant-extract creams include Camellia sinensis among botanicals studied to quench reactive oxygen species produced by UV exposure, which contributes to skin ageing.[3]

Oral green tea extract appears in supplement stacks discussed on T Nation by lifters, listed alongside fish oil, vitamins and fat-loss ingredients.[6][7] A 2022 review also reports potential use as an aid in dermatitis.[2]

Wikipedia summarizes randomized trials of green tea for non-appearance outcomes: small reductions in blood pressure (about 2 to 3 mm Hg), lower total and LDL cholesterol in a 2013 Cochrane meta-analysis, and no good evidence for weight loss.[1] A 2020 meta-analysis of cohort studies found no significant link between tea intake and colorectal cancer risk.[8]

For appearance, the evidence is mostly laboratory and in vivo antioxidant work on creams.[3] A randomized trial in untrained men tested a Camellia sinensis polyphenol blend for 28 days around resistance exercise and examined muscle signalling rather than appearance.[9] EFSA found its skin-protection claims not sufficiently supported.[1]

Excess consumption, especially of extracts, has been associated with liver toxicity and rarely liver failure; the 2022 review also raises hepatotoxicity and DNA damage concerns for extracts and main ingredients.[1][2] EFSA reported that long-term intake of extracts above 800 mg EGCG per day raised liver enzymes in some people and could not establish a safe dose; Health Canada (2017) recommended a warning label and use by adults only.[1]

A 2020 Cochrane review listed gastrointestinal effects, raised liver enzymes and, rarely, skin reactions as possible adverse effects of extracts.[1] Green tea interferes with the cancer drug bortezomib, and a 2024 review discusses possible interaction with alprazolam through CYP3A4.[1][4]

timeline.event: US FDA approves a topical green tea extract ointment as a prescription drug for genital warts.[1]
EFSA review finds most green tea health claims not sufficiently supported.[1]
Health Canada recommends a liver-related warning label for green tea extracts.[1]

card.summary: Catechin-rich antioxidant botanical common in skincare; general health claims lack strong support and oral extracts carry liver warnings.
card.note: Oral extracts linked to liver toxicity; evidence here is from a single encyclopedia summary.

quick.overview:
Green tea extract concentrates the polyphenols of green tea leaf and is used in creams, serums and supplements as an antioxidant.

Reviews summarized on Wikipedia found insufficient evidence for most claims, though one topical form is an approved prescription for genital warts.
quick.mechanism: Catechins such as EGCG are antioxidants; no proven biological effects in humans are stated for them in the source.
quick.risks: Extracts, especially oral, have been linked to liver injury; EFSA could not set a safe dose. Rare skin reactions are reported.
